BUBLIN, Nov. 2.-One civilian
was killed and a soldier and wom-
an were wounded in q fresh out
break Of reprisal violence at Tralee
today. ...


Ths soldiers and the Black and
Tan police were active throughout
Dublin. Supported by armored
cars, the troops and policemen made
numerous raids, and traffic in the
principal streets was held up for
hours. The National University
was searched, and the president,
DR.. Coffey, was placed under tenn.
porary arrest.


1 SLAY "BLACk AND TANs"


Two Black and Tan policemen were
seized at Tralee following a reprisal
attack upon the town. 1t was re.
ported that their bodies were found
riddIed with bullets, but this has not
been confined.


| When the people at Tralee awoke
this morning they found the town
filled with posters saying that un-
less the two policemen were pro-
duced. "reprisals such as Ireland has
never known before would be made
/ at Tralee ande in the vicinity"


Tho burial Of Terence McSwiney
has been followed by . wave OF vio-
ience in Ireland in which more than
q dozen persons, including half .
dozen policemen. and soldiers. were
killed and many villages were shot
liary police In reprisal attacks.


Reprisals were made by the black
and tan police despite the disciplinary
measures already taken by Sir Hamar
Greenwood, chief secretary for Ire
land. to stamp out this form OF venge-
full violence.


Among the communities that have
suffered in this latest outburst are
Tralee, West Tralee. Abbey Dorncy.
Lixaw, Listowell, Ballyduff. Thurles,
Tullamore and Dungannon.


AMBUsHED ON LONE ROADS.


British officials declare the police
were under great provocation. In ad-
dition to the policemen and soldiers
killed. ten others were wounded. some
were shot openly; others were shot
down from ambush on lonely country
roads.


Sim Fein officials declared they
were compiling documentary evidence
Of what they characterize as the wan
ton cruelty of the black and tan po-
lice. They charge that the black and
tan police brought down attacks upon
themselves by their. behavior


The warfare between the Irish Re-
publicans on one side and the SOL
diers and Black and Tan police on
the other Is shifting ireland rapidly
toward chaos. In another year the
country threatens to become a heap
| Of ashes unless peace is made. The
factories are disappearing day by
day. The people are faced with star
walton or emigration. Cities hitherto
immune from the reign of terror are
getting a strong taste of frightful-
ness.


CITIES ARMED CAMPS.


Cork, Dublin, Queenstown, Bel
fast, Londonderry, Limerick. Tip
perary. and other cities are armed
camps. There are nearly $4,000 Brit
ish soldiers massed in the country.


New forms of terror are con-
stantly entering this dreadful situ-
alton. Sim Feiners make black ac-
cusations against the military au-
thorities. and the latter reply with
charges fully as bad.


1t Is alleged by the republicans
that Q secret brigade of spies steals
nightly through this city with
siienoers attached to their auto
matte pistols, marking men for as
sassination.

when the distressed vessel, then about

Less appeals for cid. She then had on

night to the transport Northern Pa
cifc.


First Call for Help


The first radio said that the Pow
hatan was leaking, her tireroom flooded
and the vessel was being buffeted by a

hawsers.

and the Northern Pacific took off all
the passengers without accident, al
though the transfer involved the risk
and danger Of such an undertaking at
night.


The crew OF the Powhatan stuck to
the disabled ship, which was later taken
in tow by the Canadian government
steamship Lady Iaurier; The American
destroyers Leary and Sharkey assisted
the Lady Laurier in bringing the dere-
lict to port, but just as it seemed their
task would be successful another storm
came up, this time with binding snow

Again the hawsers snapped and the
Powhatan once more was adrift. In
this almost hopeless situation, Captain
Randall, commanding officer of the
Powhatan, sent radio intimating he
might have to abandon his ship owing
to her condition., which was fast be-
coming unseaworthy, and the increasing
violence Of the storm But the wealth er
calmed the next day and the Pow
hatan was put under control. With
the aid of sea going tugs, she finally
reached port at snail's place.


HALIFAX, N. S., Jan. 27--The coast
guard cutter Ossipee was almost sunk
on Saturday while trying to take the
Powhatan in tow. huge sea swept
her crashing against the Lady Lau-
rier's starboard bow, as she steamed
past to try and secure a hawser, smash
ing three boats, the port rail- part of
the pilot house and tearing away the
shrouds. The Lady Laurier suffered
no serious damage.

Jamshed tribe under it's official pro-
lection" says the London Times cor
respondent.

ain induced Russia to arrange for the
return of practically the whole tribe
to its original home in Afghanstan.

large migration of Jamshedis to soviet
territory. The bolsheviki are using
them to smuggle cattle and other sup

and Frederick 10, embarked In row.

and started out into the pond on fish

fishing from the shore around bend

irons. He. too. had been shot through

street. Recently he was arraigned in
the city court on charges of not sup
porting the children. The charges were
brought by the principal of their school.

silks has taken a squirt throughout

buying heavily for future use Even

and satinfaced goods in lighter shades

redye their lighter shades intb brown.

blue, jade. coral, orchid and peach
bloom. One of the strongest sellers is
satin-faced crepe in these colors.

stores yesterday enjoyed large busi-
ness. Managers of these departments
without exception reported that sales
double those of any day last week.
Complaints against high prices are reg
istered by customers, but they con-
tinue to buy the better class and more
expensive goods, say the retailers.

Beating the high cost of touring
proved delight to S. S. Marx, his wife
and three children, who arrived in New
York a few days ago after a trip across
the continent from Los Angeles in a
touring car and camping trailer. Their
itinerary took them through fourteen
states by what they describe as the
"dctour route"-via Arizona. New Mex
leo, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Mississippi,
Tennessee. Kentucky, Indiana, Ohio,
Pennsylvania and New Jersey. They
arc continuing the trip through New
England to Boston. and expect to re-
turn to their California home by the
northern route through Montana,
Washington and Oregon.


During the forty day trip to New
York, with numerous stops along the
way, the party slept in hotel only
once, and the total expenses were only
$500. This included meals, gasoline,
oil and repairs, and clean, comfortable,
healthful lodgings for five.


Rainy weather followed the party
nearly all the way, and heavy mud and
rutted roads were encountered in the
Mississippi Valley states, but the camp
equipment was secure and dry at all
times in the trailer The car never got
stuck so that it had to be towed out.
The only time the car failed to pull
the trailer uD hill was in Mississippi,
where a - per cent grade was struck
on a hill of loose gravel.


The camp trailer is fitted with double
woven spring beds, waterproof tent
gasoline stove, dishes, camp chairs,
folding table, shower bath and every
thing requisite for sleeping, eating and
generally living in comfort. Every
thing folds compactly within the two
wheel pneumatic-tire trailer, which
measures seven feet in length and
stands four feet high when ready for
the road

disrobed from her waist upward with

Belasco Was Enth usiastie.

performance last night. no prima
donna has been able to make
Zaza appear real. Giulio Crimi sang
the tenor role Of Dufresne and Amato

TT is not only the Chamber of Commerce
for which William S. Ware has spoken
in introducing into the House bill pro-
viding for the restoration of the pneu-
matic-tube mail service in Philadelphia.
The proposal is of general civic concern
here just as the abandonment of the
tubes in 1918 was subject of general
civic dismay.


The Burleson substitutes for the tubes
have not been popular. Reckless driving
has characterized much of the motor mail
service in this city. Prompt delivery has
become, in many instances, a mere rem
iniscence.


Philadelphia needs the tubes. In Paris
= they make for expedition in the local
postal service in way which delightfully."-
startles our natives abroad. But they
are less indispensable in the French cap
ital, with its wide avenues and boule-
wards, than in checkerboard Philadelphia
with its narrow streets and increasingly
congested traffic.


The sooner the perverse act of suspend
ing the tube deliveries is nullified the
better for postal system that has been
ruthlessly shedding its medals through
out the Wilson administration.

bandits and japanese troops. About

garrison on the night of the 9Th, but

arrived from Ranan to reinforce the
garrison. On the following morning

twenty clashed with Japanese force
at a point some 1000 meters north of
Ansan. but were defeated. The jap
anese pursued the Koreans, when
another group of Koreans occupying
a table land in the vicinity fired on
the Japanese. They were driven off
after about four hours hard resist
ance, leaving twenty-four dead and
quantity OF arms and ammunition,
The Japanese casualties were sixty
two.


The garrison commander the same
day issued an order which said:


1.-The present Korean outbreak made
it inevitable for the Japanese to enter
Chinese territory, since the rioters
made their way into the Japanese
garrisoning quarters from within Chi
nese territory"

LONDON, July S.-Edward Albert,
Prince Of Wales. emerged unscathed
and smiling through the window Of
an overturned car when his train was
wrecked yesterday, says a dispatch
from Perth, Australia, to the London
Times.


The accident occurred near Bridge
town, West Australia, according to
the report. The princes parlor car
and one adjoining, which were last in
the train. were derailed, dragged for
200 yards and then overturned. Soon
after climbing from the wreck the
prince was joking and good-naturedly
chatting the West Australian premier
and other officials accompanying him.
He was cheered by the crowd that
witnessed his dramatic escape from
the wreck.


Some members of the princes staff
received bruises of slight nature.

Unostentatiously included in the
annual report of the Surgeon-General
of the Navy for the last fiscal year is
the subjoined account of the splendid
conduct of the crew of the United
States ship vicksburg In our northern
Pacific waters:


During the month of June tho
Vicksburg was engaged in relief


work In connection with the influenza
epidemic on the Alaskan peninsula.


y. "At Akutan and Ugashik 1t was


found that the entire population of


the villages was sick and many had
already succumbed to the disease not
a single inhabitant was well enough
to care for himself or others.


They were practically without


food AMI sanitary conditions were


extremely deplorable.


sit was apparent that IL the en-


tire determination of the natives was


to be prevented the ship must not


only feed them and extend medical


treatment. but sufficient men must be


landed from the ship to nurse the


entire population.


Volunteers were called for. and


out OF practically the entire ships


company that volunteered fourteen


were accepted


''They prepared food, nursed the


sicls buried the dead and improved


the sanitary conditions"


No man or woman can read this
simple record of unassuming heroism
without thrilling with pride ut the
splendid spirit which inspired all the
men who volunteered for this depress-
ing and laborious task-"practically
the entire ships cornpany"-and the
magnificent devotion which sustained
those who were chosen for the work.


Let nobody be deceived as to the ma.
ture of their labors. For men held to
the standard Of cleanliness and pro
vided with the instruments Of mod
ern sanitation which are character
istic of the American Navy TO quit
their ship for the primitive and unin-
viting shore of Alaska, and there to
nurse the stricken natives, to cook for
them, to struggle to improve the sani-
tary conditions among them, and to
bury their dead, entailed sacrifices of
comfort, of physical well being, of
bodily safety which only the highest
courage and the most unfiinching for
titude could endure.


They exchanged regularity and COM
fort on board ship for the hardships
and actual dangers on land, making
the choice freely and sacrificing them
selves cheerfully for people to them
unknown and without particular
appeal.


That men should strive to gain q
place on the Merrimac when HoBsoN
headed her for the channel of Santi-
ago harbor, when death might come
to them from the cannon of their
country's foe, required bravery. For
men to seek the danger zone when
lurking submarines infested the seas
called for bravery. And bravery as
fine as any man can show was needed
to send the men OF the Vicksburg
ashore In Alaska, there, under the
most distressing conditions, to toll
laboriously for the dying natives and
those whose bodies death had already
claimed.


Ideallsm? Perhaps none of the hun
dreds who boldly volunteered ever
used that word. But where has hui
man service ever had finer exemplars
than among these unnamed American
sailormen Of the United States ship
Vicksburg?

LONDON, Sept. 15.-The prospects
of settlement of the differences be-
tween the government and the coal
miners and the prevention of their
threatened strike were vastly improved
to-day. The Cabinet conferred at two
long sessions lasting most of the day.
Premier Lloyd George spent two hours
with the ministers.


A conference between the government
and representatives of the Miners
Federation is expected soon. Lloyd
Georges letter, in which he said that
the government would exercise control
over coal until the export price approx
mated more closely the home price,
and the letter from Robert Smillie,
president Of the Miners Federation, to
The Times, in which he said that the
controversy was not political and that
the question of naturalization was not
involved, may be considered as steps
toward a compromise. They indicate
the desire of both sides to reach a set
tlement before the expiration of the
notice served by the miners, nine days
hence.


The governments plans for keeping
the food supply channels open are being
enlarged constantly and the authorities
are confident that they can handle the
situation however long the strike might
last.


Several large industrial organizations
have notified their employees that they
will shut down Immediately if the min
ers' strike takes place. Others will oper-
ate as long as the fuel lasts, dropping
their employees as it becomes neces-
sary to shut down.

The allies, General Estienne now

flowing river Rhine-by the use or

infantry were crossing In boats.


The idea OF these crawling mon
sters, says General Estienne, dates
back several years. but he and other
French inventors only concentrated
their minds upon the subject when
the caterpillar tank was proved sue
oessful in land warfare.

optimistic allied chieftains were ceD-

the. winter. The general impression
was that allied arms would have
scored a great success had Luden-
dorff been forced to retire to the
Rhine to shorten his line and there
appeared for the supreme defense in
the spring OF 1919.


The difficulties that the allies would
have faced in crossing the Rhine were
fully realized by Marshal Foch. 1t
was during the summer OF 1918, ac-
cording to General Estinne, the plan
OF using crawling. swimming mon
sters, equipped with machine guns
and small bore pieces of artillery was
discussed and approved. The allies,

moral effect the unexpected appear
ance OF these turtle tanks" in the

The steamship Deepwater came off
Sandy Hook yesterday on her way from
Genoa towing the schooner Rostellan,
which had been adrift about 500 miles
east of Bermuda for eight weeks.
Laden, with palm oil and ivory, the Ros-
tellan sailed out of Loango on her jour
nev to Liverpool.


When two weeks on the Atlantic she
encountered a storm which ripped her
sails to shreds and carried away her
rudder. Terrific seas washed over her
decks, sweeping with them all deck
gear and fittings, but, fortunately, the
pounding did not open up the schooner's
seams Flares we're burned at night
and throughout the day a careful watch
was kept for a passing steamship.


Several times the men of the Ros-
tellan sighted streak of smoke on the
horizon, but the ship that sent it up
did not come their way. Occasionally
they were able to make out the masts
of a steamship, but the vessel passed
on without observing them.


The supply of food and water on the
derelict held out well, and on February
18, when the men were down to their
last gallon Of water, the Deepwater was
sighted to the eastward She was
heading northeast, and it was feared
aboard the Rostellan that she, too,
might pass by without observing them.


Presently she changed her course and
bore down upon the helpless schooner,
and within three hours after her ar
rival she had the Rostellan in tow
The master and crew and dog and a
goat were taken aboard the Deepwater
before she took hold of the derelict.

/ believe there is an explanation

white man.


1t Is terrible story of reversion
to primitive passions. But the white
man. suddenly confronted with an

most invariably is brutalized until

orous protest fifteen years ago. were

tiplied indefinitely.


The Haitian revelations show
Americans at home that the white
man seems the universal victim OF

are scarcely 1900 years removed

years formed our instincts and
guided our habits.


But, the higher civilization dem
onstrates it's fitness, nevertheless.
For. the white man no longer allows

white man, himself. stops them. His

The rescue. effected by tunnelins

The men We're trapped three miles

After all other attempts at rescue

Tor the miners. The rescue party,

go to the end of the mine in an at

fire soon enough to make his escape.

cue teams from nearby coal mining
cities were called on for assistance.


The rescue teams worked tirelessly

the men would still be alive when
reached.

Huddled together in a little group
near the blazing entrance of the mine
this morning were the wives and
; families of the entrapped men. They
had kept a sorrowful and tireless vigil
throughout the night in the faint
hope that their loved ones would be


The whites and blacks were drawn
together in the disaster affecting
both. Grief-stricken and weeping
they stood. watching the smoke pour
from the burning mine. forming an
incentive to greater efforts by the
reScuerS


The fire was started from defective
electric wiring in room near the
opening. and quickly spread. The
plant is drift mine with no shafts.

mine rescue section of theSPittsburgh

Elephants are the only animals
that deliberately wash themselves
in water. Female African elephants
have been seen to daub their calves
with mud and then wash it off, ap-
parently soaping and sluicing their
young.


Most naked skin animals love to
wallow in water or mud and water.
and some furred animals also do.
Such bathing is enjoyed by the rhi-
nosceros and buffalo. bears, tigers,
and dogs. But this wallowing is not
bathing. Indeed. the animals are
sometimes dirtier afterward than
before.


Some animals, such as cats and
mice, do all their bathing by lick
ing. Game birds favor a roll in
sand, although some keep their
coats sleek without either dry or
wet cleaning.


Birds appear to be the chief water
washers. Some of them prefer
shower baths, such as are possible
during rain storms, and they enter
into their bath with great glee.
Some delight in dust baths, while
some few. like the sparrow, employ
both dust and water.

automobile, which was left with en-

the other two robbers went through
their pockets. and compelled them
to slip off diamond rings.


Slowly backing towards the door,
one of the bandits said:


IF anyone makes a noise inside
of five minutes he'll be a dead man"


AS the four men backed into the
street they ran into a man who lives
in the neighborhood. He started to
grapple with one of the thieves, but
was soon thrust aside and the quar-
tet then made a run for their
waiting automobile.


Police commandeercd an automo-
bile and started after the fugitive
car. -


The high-powered touring car
occupied by the bandits soon out
distanced the pursuers. Later po-
lice placed under arrest two men
believed to know something of the
robbery.

were transferred to police launch and
taken to the Morgue.

Juan s. Gomas of 526 Greenwich street

riguez, 81 years old. Rodriguez came
here three weeks ago from British
Guiana. The two other men appeared
to be Manuel Torres, aged 40, married,
500 Greenwich street, and Figuero Fa-
rina, 30, married. of 400 West street.

room cleaners, and were not members
of the crew.

Sixteen men of the American steam

by a mine off the Netherlands coast
December 5, arrived here yesterday on
the transport Mercury, with an odd tale
of the disaster\


The Liberty Clio, they said, had had
serene trip ON her journey to Bre-
men until she hit the mine, about
twenty-five miles off Armuland Light
house. The mine hit her near the
bridge, tearing her in two sections.
The stout keel, however, refused to let
the two portions separate and the
bulkhead held out the flood. Although
cut into two sections above the water
line, the skipper kept his craft under
way and dropped anchor at 5 p M,
when within seven miles of the light.
Her wireless calls for help had been
answered, and with this assurance
many of the crew turned in for the
night.


Meanwhile heavy storm with snow
and sleet came up from the north, and
the high seas snapped the keel that

boats and rowed seven miles to the
beach.


The first boat over the side jammed
and tossed three men into the sea, but
they were later picked up. Including
the master, the Liberty Clio carried
forty-three men, and forty-one men in
three lifeboats were landed on the
shore. Four men were frozen to death

Eleventh Avenue, which has been
waiting for a good opportunity to
"jump cop" ever since Charles Tucker
was shot accidentally by patrol
man July 5, decided that its chance
had come late yesterday afternoon
when Patrolman John j. Farrell start
ed down that thoroughfare from Fiji
tieth Street with three prisoners.


They were Michael Reilly, Of $40

Gated on the sidewalk, the patrolman

vile Farrell when he asked what

Quite aware of the peril that lurked

to walk ahead. Before they had gone
dozen PAGES they were the center Oh
q group whose rearmost members be-
gan to jeer the patrolman, several
Shouting: That's the cop that got
Tucker"


At Fortv-ninth Street a pair of
br.wny arms seized the patrolman
from behind and tore him away from
his prisoners. In a moment he was
the center OF a shouting, list brand
ishing mob, which, led. Farrell asserts,
by ms prisoners, began to pummel
and kick him. He drew his revolver,
using It alternately as a billy and to
cover the three men whom he had
arrested.


Some one gave him crack with
club that made his head spin and at
the same instant the man who had
precipitated the attack snatched Far
rell's revolver. The patrolman was
staggering from the blows ralned
upon him, when a member of the
police reserves who had pressed close
to nina during the struggle, though
without offering to take sides against
his neighbors, thrust an automatic
pistol into Farrel's hand


With this he forced Foley and Nc
Cabe ahead of him into the tenement
into which Reilly had lodged the in
slant that the patrolman faltered.
Having seen the pistol in Farrell's
hand. the crowd hesitated to follow
him into the basement house, and
without interference Farrell and his
prisoners conducted the search for
Reilly.


They found him crouching on fire
escape, whence Farrell drew him none
too gently and lined him up beside
his companions against the wall of a
hallway. He kept them there under
the muzzle of his pistol. The tenement
hallway was the safest place and the
easiest to defend that he had seen
since leaving Fiftieth Street, and he
resolved to wait there until word Of
his plight got to the police.


1t was only few minutes before the
reserves from the West Forty -seventh
Street police station, has had two men
through the mob at the entrance to
the tenement. leaving broken heads in
their wake. Farrell and his three pris-
oners were escorted to the police sta
ton.


Although dazed from the blow on the
head and otherwise battered, Farrell
remained on duty. The man who
seized him from behind and snatched
his revolver got away in the confu-
sion. Until few days ago Captain
McCauley, of the West Forty seventh
Street police station has had two men
assigned to the post Farrell had yes
terday because of the threats that had
been made that "some cop would get
his" for the shooting of Tucker

SPA. July 9.-All obstacles to closer

note received to-day from Moscow by

tives here. Soviet Russia accepts all
British proposals which Leonid Kras-
sin took from London to Moscow.


The Bolshevik reply, according to the
plan, was to be sent here.


The Bolsheviki accept the British
stipulations that the Soviets release
all prisoners, withdraw from Persia
and recognize the commercial rights of
British individuals in Russia.

An armistice between the union
lists in Guatemala and forces of
President Estrada Cabrera has
been signed and the proposal made
that President Cabrera leave the
country, according to advices today
to the State Department.


The armistice' resulted from
conference requested by both sides
held at the American legation in
Guatemala City. in which the en-
tire diplomatic corps participated.
The suggestion that President Ca
brera leave the country was made by
the unionist leaders. who guaranteed
safe conduct for him and his family.


The unionist movement was
launched last week, and the capital
was captured after some street
fighting President Cabrera held
the forts and heights dominating
the place. but did not permit his
main force to resist the unionists
when they entered Guatemala
City.

ANNAPOLIS, Md, Feb. 17.Within

was rejected by both House and Senate.

Senate: Eighteen against and nine
for ratification. House: Sixty-four
against and thirty-six for ratification.

State House was crowded with suf-
fragists and anti-suffragists. The for
men brought a band from Baltimore,
which played popular airs in the cor
ridor. Before the vote Governor Ritchie
received call from the suffragists, who
criticized his stand on the amendment.

matter would not come to him for ap-
proval or disapproval.

NEW YORK, Sept. 3.-Four Of
ficers and twenty-four men, the crew
of the United States submarine SIS,
arc safe today after submersion in
their disabled vessel more than thir-
ty-five hours off the Delaware capes.


A radio message received early to-
day at the Brooklyn Navy Yard said
the merchant ship Alantheus was
towing the disabled undersea boat to
the Delaware breakwater.


SAVED BY PHONE BUOY.


The plight of the SIS was discover
ed when the George w. Goethals, an
American vessel. saw a telephone
buoy floating from the submarine.
The buoy was ringing and a small
boat was lowered from the Goethale.


The telephone operator in the sub
marine said the vessel had been dis
abled then for thirty-five hours. She
was almost vertical. making 1T i'm
possible to release any of tho crew
through the torpedo tubes, which are
in the bow.


A later message from the telephone
operator said the submarines air was
being exhausted. Divers then were
lowered from the Cocktails. small
hole was cut in the submarines hull,
and an air hose inserted.


Later cables were passed about the
submerged vessel to hold 1t from
sinking farther.


DEsTROYERs TO RESCUE.


Communications to naval stations
sent destroyers rushing to the scene.
Only the most meager word had been
received from these ships early today,
their messages merely stating that
the men and officers all were safe and
were on their way to the Delaware

thorities in the occupied and plebes-

vent the collection of the German
income tax on wages in the dis
tricts under their control. The pro-
visions of the new income law re-
quiring employers to deduct a fiat
10 per cent from all salaries and
wages goes into effect on June 25.


The workmen are very bitter over
the new imposition and the entente
authorities apparently fear that
strikes will result from an attempt
to enforce the law. The workmen
and others with small salaries look
upon fiat deduction as an injustice,
since under the progressive gradu-
alton of the tax they usually are
liable for less than 10 per cent, par
ticularly when the exemption for
the family is considered.


Workmen with small incomes,
therefore, are virtually compelled
to make a forced loan to the state
until the next year. when the excess
over the actual tax will be refund
ed, whereas the deduction is felt
less severely by those with larger
incomes, on which the tax runs well
over 10 per cent.

Mary Seaman, twelve years old, of

play anything from jazz to grand opera,

WASHINGTON, April 14.-An armi-
stice between the Unionists in Qua
temala and forces of President
ESTRADA Cabrera has been signed and

orera leave the country, according to
advices to-day to the State Depart
ment.

ference requested by both sides. held
at the American Legation. in Guate-
mala City, in which the entire diplo-
matte corps participated. The sug-
gestlon that President Cabrera leave
the country was made by the Unionist
leaders, who guaranteed safe conduct
for him and his family.


Ihe Unlonlst movement was launched
last week and the capital was captured
after some street fighting.


The conference at the American
Legation was held last Sunday night.
The Guatemalan Minister of Foreign
Affairs proposed that acts of the
Guatemalan Congress April s, directed
against President Cabrera, be declared
void. that the President convene the
legislative branch of the government
to receive his resignation, and that
General Mariana Serrano Munzo be
vested with constitutional powers as
President designado.


The State Department has been in
formed that before these negotiations
there had been a considerable exchange
of shots. Many shells passed over the
city April 10 and several were reported
to have struck the Brazilian Legation.
which led to protest by the diplomatic
corps. The firing was then suspended
but was resumed April II.

LONDON, July 15.-There seems to
be no limit to the audacity of the Sim
Fem. All Dublin is laughing tonight
while the police and military are com
pietely baffled over this mornings "out-
rage" when the general postofice in
Dublin was raided shortly after z
O'Clock by band of fifty Sim Feiners
many of whom made no effort to dis
guise themselves.


Official correspondence only was
stolen. The first intimation that the
postal clerks--about 200 of them, who
were sorting the early morning mail
had that anything was wrong was
when fifteen masked Sim Feiners
popped into the main lobby of the
postoffice through letter chute, one
after the other.


There are five telephones in the Dublin
postoffice and ten of these unexpected
visitors made Immediately for the in
struments, two mounting guard over
each. The remaining five who were
joined by eight who came in through
the employees entrance, made straight
for the "state" section, where official
correspondence is dealt with. Skilfully
and with apparent knowledge of the
workings of the postoffice, the masked
men selected certain stacks of police and
military mail, flung them into sacks and
departed.


The raid occupied less than ten min
utes. The postal workers were covered
by the men at the phones and offered no
resistance. One man refused to help
the raiders sort letters.


When the sacks had been carried to
the door of the postoffice a whistle
summoned a motor car, which quickly
whirled the half dozen leaders and
their booty away from the scene of the
raid. The other Sim Feiners who had
been idly standing guard in an infor-
NAL Gordon around the postoffice dis
persed and disappeared by the simple
process of mingling with the crowd
which had gathered.


Not the sligHest attempt was made
to interfere with the work of the raid
ers or to inform the military police.
The postoffice occupies the site of the
former skating rink in Pannell Square,
within a stones throw of Sackville
Street, Dublin's busiest thoroughfare.


The correspondent of "The Westmin-
ster Gazette" tonight reports from
Cork that the rebuffs which the Sim
Fem agitation for independence met
with in America have not in any way
discouraged the Republican rank and
file The people of the South, he says,
firmly believe that they are winning
and that the government eventually
Will tire Of the struggle.


Recruiting for the Republican army
continues apace and it is suggested
that spectacular Sim Fein outrages
many of them comparatively harmless
IN themselves, are proving great boon
In this recruiting, the imagination of
young Irish farmers being fired by the
stories of these deeds. Many youthful
adherents, it is said, have been gained
by attacks on empty police barracks

The 1ncas have long been celebrated In

Mr.. valderrama, it is said. lived with the

bamboo rods of varying lengths and re.
sembling flutes. AS they were animistic ir
their belief, each note of their music was
invested with characteristic meaning.

lions typrylng the Punitive age. They
were morning prayer to the sun, ar
Inca royal dance, love song, a legend
and the conquest. The second part of his
programme typified the colonial age and
included the Peruvian Native Air" and
the present day characteristic Peruvian
Waltz"

based were most interesting, vastly more
so than the music itself. There was char.
acteristic Indian rhythm and monoton.
Gus interminable repetition. Evidently
when the Inca found few intervals tc
his liking he repeated them incessantly
Mr.. Valderrama was not guided by present
day artistic standards in his arrangement,
of these melodies He showed weakness
in inventive skill. especially in his har
nominations for bass. His arrangement.
were shallow bombastic, with a predilec.
tion for snowy passage work for the most
part meaningless, save wherein the sue
cessive octaves reaching higher ano
higher, the varying flute lengths sug.
gested themselves.

BERLIN, March 16.-Probably one
reason for Chancellor Kapp's changed
attitude is the frmness shown by the
workingmen in repudiating him by
their widespread strike. The walls of
buildings here are placarded with the
appeals of dozen great labor organi-
cations, urging their members to re-
main on strike everywhere until con-
stitutional conditions are restored.


There Is nowhere in Berlin among
the workingmen any disposition to
invite an attack from the revolutionary
forces which the reactonaries obvi-
ously are using to overawe them
Troops are parading the principal
streets, flying the old naval flag and
demonstrating their equipment of artil-
lery and machine guns.


The strike has reached unprecedent-
ed dimensions. All the streetcars
omnibusses and subways are idle and
nearly all the shops are closed, but the
banks still are open. The problem is
growing acute for hotel guests, as
kitchens and dining rooms are closing
and the servants are striking. The
Tribune correspondent made his owr
bed to-day. Water, light and heat have
stopped.


great run was made this morning
on groceries, and the bakeries were
stormed for bread and sold out by 9
o'clock. 1t is asserted that Berlin is
provisioned for only one day. Railway
service has suspended, but food trains
will continue to run. Berlin's streets
are wholly without traffic.

fleet will be granted fifteen-day leaves
to visit their homes throughout the
country between now and the first OF
the year.

sections. entered the ports of New

battleships and eighteen destroyers

Full compliments will be restored
with the coming of the new year, and
on January 3 the four sections will
go to sea again, meeting off the Nir-
ginia capes January 5, for a trip to
bay, Cuba, and later to
the Canal Zone. where the Pacific
leet will join the Atlantic warships
January "a.

airy, the Atlantic fleet will steam to
Guantanamo bay, Cuba, for annual
target practice. remaining away until
May 1, when the ships will again re-
turn to their home yards.

Large lung capacity. light bones and

sary for speed in swimming, accord
swimming instructor, who will be-
gin swimming instructions at the
tidal basin bathing beach Sunday.
Women should also be better swim
mers than men because their bodies
are of higher specific gravity Mr..
iCorsan says.


There are various reasons for this"
he says. Bodies of men are chiefly
composed of heavy muscular tissue,
while the bodies of women are over
laid with a smooth buoyant sheath of
adipose tissue faD. A pail of lean
meat will sink rapidly in salt water.

float, even in fresh water. Moreover,
lung capacity is a more potent factor

other physical attribute.


zone who can inhale 400 cubic

light bone structure and enough fat

ease. Others having enormous mus

cious lungs. Long, wide, fiat feet aid

special structural advantages with
style added thereto.

worked for years at the crawl
stroke and never won a race of any
account, simply because Mother Ma
ture has not formed him to the
swimming shape-that of sea lion
Growing children who practice swim
ming assiduously during their
growth develop smoothness, lung
capacity, acquire correct style and

The angular persons. whose bones

LONDON, Sept. 1.-The British in
dustrial situation Is extremely grave,

The chief reason for optimism Is the
knowledge that the British generally
reach q compromise when danger
threatens all classes.


The Triple Alliance, a gigantic COM
bination of union workers, met again
to-day after deciding that the coal
miners demands were both reasonable
and just, but the leaders are simply
marking time, hoping that the govern
ment will make a move which will re-
lieve them from the responsibility Of
throwing the whole country into chaos
through stoppage of all work.


Sir Robert Horne, who is acting for
the Cabinet, seemed confident that tho
workers leaders would approach MIN
with an offer which might serve az the
basis of negotiations and eventually Of
a settlement of the differences. Robert
Smile, president of the Miners Fed
eratlon, has won the moral support OF
leaders outside the coal trade, but
nevertheless there is little sentiment
favoring strike even among workers,
who would suffer just as much as the
dsinterested public.


Tomorrow is the date fixed for hand
ing in the strike notice, which would
expire on September IS, provided no
settlement is reached meanwhile.


LONDON. Sept. (By The Associ-
ated Press).-The Evening News as
serts tonight the Triple Alliance Of
labor-the railwaymen, transport work
ers and miners-will not adopt media
ton between the miners and the gov
eminent. On the contrary, the news
paper says the railwaymen and trans
port workers have pledged full and
active support to the miners should a
strike be decided upon at to-morrow's
conference Of delegates of the three
unions.

In recent speech the Democratic
candidate for Vice-President, FRANK
LIN ID. ROOSEVELT, declared that he
had concrete plan for decreasing the
cost Of living. One of his bright ideas
was the opening up of great tracts Of
new land for the farmer.


The foolishness Of such talk is en-
phasized by the reports Of the Census
Bureau on urban and rural popula-
tons. Ten years ago the cities had
nearly 100000 fewer people than the
country. To-day the inhabitants Of
the cities outnumber the country peo-
pie by 100000.


Professor HoBsoN of Columbia
makes the drift to the cities appear
even more remarkable. His figures
show that a hundred years ago 81 per
cent. Of Americans lived directly Off
the soil. To-day less than 80 per cent
are engaged In agriculture.


What the farmers need for the gen
eral good Is not more land but more
men. They will get them when the
working hours, pay and conveniences
OF the farm overbalance urban attrac-
lions. Meanwhile the cities will have
to pay well for their food because
their very pleasantness has lured
young men from the plough.

forks of streams. for saw mills. In

churches and graveyards the were do
ing what the geologists are doing now

MADRID, July 12.-The former
Empress Eugenie OF France died
here yesterday. She was the widow
Of Napoleon III.


The former Empress was III only q
few hours before her death. She was
exceptionally well Saturday morning.
At midday she lunched heartily, eat
ing chicken and some ham.


A short time later she became III,
experiencing severe abdominal pain.
DR.. Grenda, physician TO King Al
fonso, was called and, finding her
condition serious, summoned DIR. Mo-
rena Zancudo. a specialist, and also
two other physicians. They were,
however, unable to relieve the pa
tient.


Empress Eugenia seemed conscious
that death was approaching, and
those who stood by the bedside say
she appeared glad to die in Spain, her
native country.


Saturday afternoon when the condi-
tion of Eugenie became worse, all her
relatives still in Spain were notified.
The Duchess Sahtona with her hus-
band arrived. and then the Duke of
Penerando, Dowager Duchess Tan
ames and the Count and Countess
Mora.


During the night the Empress lost
consciousness. but before doing so re-
.ceived the last sacraments of the
church from a clergyman. Eugenie
died shortly before 8 o'clock Sunday
morning, never having regained con-
sciousness.


The body will be embalmed Monday
in preparation for its transportation
to England, where Eugenie win be
buried at Marlborough. The funeral
party will probably depart for Spain
Wednesday.

discovered Miss Oberly unconscious

Indications were that she had strug-
gled desperately with her attackers.

feeling that the wet and dry issue had
been successfully evaded, it was up

caused the deadlock.


Back OF the opposition to Gov. Cox
was the dry strength. Supporting
Gov. Cox were the wet states. The
Cox managers believed it was strategy
to help omit the prohibition plank
from the platform on the ground that
their candidate, being regarded as a
wet, would satisfy the demands of
the vets. But while New Jersey and
New York and Illinois were largely
for Cox, they met obstacles from the
western dry states.


Sore spots developed among the
democrats and it was largely because

We are not among those who attribute
high prices wholly to widespread extravaganza
since the war. Undue extravaganza is prac-
ticed only in exceptional instances. Many
whose incomes have greatly increased do de-
mand fine things and luxuries which they
could not afford before the war. But the
average citizen and his wife find it none too
easy to buy all they need, of the quality they
long ago learned to appreciate, Nevertheless,
the natural human desire for better things,
among those who make more money than for
merly, may be one of the many causes under
lying higher prices


The "profiteering" and the high-price era
began with the absolute necessity for speed in
the enormous and marvellous WORK OF
EQUIPPING OUR ARMY AND NAVY. Big
profits and unheard-0f wages had to be granted
to get quick action. Afterward came the utter
depletion of surplus goods and CURTAIL-
MENT OF PRODUCTION due to the divert
ing of most industries to producing war ma
terias.


After the armistice there was somewhat
general tendency toward caution and conserva-
tisn, and belief that prices would fall. Some
folks forgot that inevitable law of SUPPLY
AND DEMAND. Some merchants stayed out
of the market for awhile, and here and there
early in 1919 manufacturers began to quote
prices little lower. But the great consuming
public was asking for merchandise. Retailers
had to order goods. Soon notifications began
to come that orders would be delayed or only
partially filled. Demand exceeded supply
Prices, instead of falling, continued to rise
Labor demanded higher pay, and got it-got it
again and again. And there's no immediate
sign that prices are going to drop.

Sir: When our forefathers gath

the tyrannical conduct of George III.

The early history Of our country
shows with what jealousy and zeal the
people held to this feature of the gov
ernment. Thomas Jefferson arose with
his democratic banner of pure and SIM
pie democracy and subdued under his
heel the Virginia clique that were
alternating the Presidents chair and
removing it from the public pulse.


The present Administration has shown
that the peoples eyes and hearts, while
totally obsessed with the gigantic
struggle against imperialism and kai-
serlsm, have overlooked the ominous
tendencies here right at home. onder
guise of war emergency the Presiden-
tial prerogative has been magnified
tremendously so as to strike at the
base Of the foundation Of our con-
stltutlonal freedom.


The President has gathered upon
himself the absolute rule of the Cabi-
net and so restricted, cajoled and
forced their will that the executive
department of the government has
risen in revolt and refused to be
shackled. The department chiefs
freedom Of action has been strangled

the distribution of coal supplies from
the Ruhr fields to the South German
districts. 1t is expected that the ship
ments of American coal up the Rhine
10 Mannheim factories that began sew
eral months ago will cease soon


Under these circumstances the whole
industrial region of Germany is hard
hit Many of the plants derive their
power from hydro-electric stations on
tae Rhine and these have been COM
PEELED by the low water level to run
only on short shifts In South Ger
many the mountain brooks have stopped

population.

centric and rich widow with one baby
daughter Beatrice.


Beatrice was her mothers sole
heiress, and was destined to vast
wealth aud high social position. Her
mother feared these prospects might
spoil the child's nature. And she
sought for a way to prevent It.


The problem found a queer solu-
ton when Beatrice was barely two
years old. At that time Lady Mildred
adopted another little girl, the same
age as her own daughter.


The adopted child was Polly honu-
ment, daughter of a former servant
of Lady Mildred's.


The eccentric widow brought up tbs
two girls as sisters, not telling either
OF them which one was Beatrice, the
heiress, and which one was Polly, the
servants child.


She called them 'rViolet'' and Val
entine." and treated them Just alike.
giving each of them all possible ad-

When the two girls were twenty
years old, Lady Mildred took them
both to call on Polly's family In ~
humble and crowded home they So
occupied.


Violet shrank with horror from
meeting the family. She troubled lest
she herself should happen to be the

But Valentine took quite another
view OF the matter. II she ware,

In this way she and Claude were

family, still helping them and seeing

In course of time she and Claude
fell overwhelmingly in love with each
other. And, with Lady Mildred's

The totem poles are going. These
quaint monuments OF a vanishing
race that have made the coast OF
British Columbia and southern Alaska
famous are fast wasting under the
influence of wind and weather.


Once the designing and construct
ing of totem poles flourished among
the Haidas and to a lesser extent
among the Tsimpsean Indians. This
was long before the white man in
vaded the Pacific northwest. Real
totem poles with the history of
tribes and families carved into their
odd structures are no longer made
and each year sees some of the older
ones disappear. Some are still stand
ing in their original positions in the
village of Kitwanga, on the Skeena
river Some of these are said to be
zoo years old.

PATERSON, N. j., May 24.-Mrs.
Edna Mensing, seventeen years old, of
COS Main Street, has awakened her hus-
band Henry, thirty-two, several times
by clicking an unloaded revolver along
side his head. The snap Of the hammer
generally awakened him more effectu-
ally than the ordinary alarm clock
could do.


This morning, at o'clock, Mrs.
Mensing put the barrel of the revolver
against her husbands temple and
pulled the trigger, There was a re-
port and the husband sank back on
his pillow. He was shot through the
brain and died instantly.


The wife ran screaming to the room
of her grandmother, Mrs. Annabelle
Getta, seventy-five, and asked her to
call physician.


The unexploded cartridges and one
empty shell were found in the re-
volver. Mrs. Mensing was charged
with murder, and entered plea of not
guilty before Recorder William Young.
Mrs. Mary Loges, her mother, was pa
rolled as material witness, as was
Mrs. Getta, the grandm other. The
husband was carpenter in a brewery.
The couple were married last New
Years Eve The police are inclined to
accept Mrs. Mensing's explanation of
the shooting.

"Jim" swallowed, head first, another
brook trout weighing more than a
pound.

PHILADELPHIA, March g. Jimmy
Wilde, the British fyweight champion,
outfought and outpointed Patsy Wal
lace, of Philadelphia, in a fast six
round bout here tonight. Wallace
fought hard battle against the cham
pion, and almost scored knockdown in
the last round


The first and sixth rounds were even.
while the British boxer easily led in
the intervening four rounds. Wilde
felt out the Philadelphia boxer in the
first round, but in the second the Brit
ish titleholder opened his attack with
mixture of snappy left hooks and
jabs and straight lefts. He had Wal
lace's nose bleeding freely. Wallace
fought back punch for punch.


In the next three rounds Wilde
demonstrated that he was the better
boxer. Wallace appeared to have more
power in his punches, but did not land
as frequently as his opponent. At the
end of the fifth round Wildes mouth
was bleeding.


The sixth round found both fighters
eager to mix it up. The Philadelphia
boy made wonderful rally. In the
middle of the round he crossed q right
hook on Wilde's left cheek bone. Wilde
fell forward and came down on his
finger tips, but was up instantly. The
big crowd cheered and franticaIly
yelled for the Philadelphian to land
knockout, but the British champion
came back with a fusillade Of rights
and lefts.

Robert Gautier. a pilot OF the New
York Washington air mail service.
whose plane crashed to earth at Col
lege Park, Md, as he was leaving for
New York last Monday, died this
morning at Emergency Hospital from
burns received In the accident.


Gautier was twenty-three years old
and saw active air Service during the
war, having won several medals for
the daring work with the French
forces. He came to this country
February !, and since February 20
has been in Washington. He entered
the air service a few weeks ago.


Officials at the flying station. where
Gautier received his injuries, state
that the aviator was being tested for
the aerial mail service and was sent
up in machine with which he was
not entirely familiar. Being caught
in the rain. he attempted to reach the
landing field, but miscalculated the
distance, and when nearing the
ground, the landing gear of his ma
chine struck the wires Of the radio
station. and the machine caught fire,
falling to the ground.


Gautier was burned about the head
and chest before he could loosen his
life belt and crawl from the wreck
age. He was removed to Emergency
Hospital. after the accident.


Funeral arrangements have not
been announced.

escorting about twenty prisoners across
the campus.

alarm until she had got the others
safely into building. Meanwhile. the
fugitives had waded through slush and
mud, climbed fences and penetrated
thick underbrush until they reached
the summer home of Henry Howe.

moned his hired men, and they formed

did not care to face. They turned

McDougall's Pond, on which children
of Brooklyn have skated and slid all
winter, lay deserted last night. Near
the center Of the dark stretch of ice at
Ninth Avenue and Forty-seventh Street
was darker, jagged hole, and in his
home, at 931 Third Avenue, Frank
Sagona. eleven years old and hero,
buried his face in his pillow and sobbed
himself to sleep.


The pond drew it's usual quota of
youngsters with sled and skates yester-
day afternoon. Frank and $his chum,
Danny Derosa, likewise eleven, of 34l
Thrty-sxth Street, went there together.
The warmth and ran of the last few
days and turned the ice Timber" and
the children at their play clung close
to the shore line.


All except Danny. He strapped on
his skates and glided out toward the
center of the pond, laughing as the ice
creaked and gave beneath him.


Jaw, come on, you 'fraid cats!" he
shouted over his shoulder. "It's
smoother out here. It's swell!"


Suddenly Danny wasn't there-only
hole with black water tapping its
edges. Then his head reappeared and
he clung to the treacherous rim of the
hole, but the ice gave way and down
he went again.


The children were screaming, panic
stricken. John Derosa, Danny's brother,
was running toward the nearest tele-
phone, but Frank Sayona was moving in
the other direction. With piece of
tape in his hand, he was creeping out
over the ice toward the hole where his
pal was drowning.


He tossed one end of the tape to the
struggling boy, who clutched at it and
caught it. Then Frank pulled, but the
ice beneatah his own feet gave way
with him and plunged him in beside
his friend. Neither of the lads could
swim, but Frank slipped an arm over
the ice ledge and fastened his other
hand in Danny's collar. Once more
the ice broke and he went down. When
he came to the surface and clutched
the ice again Danny had DISAPPEARED.

Witnesses before the Congressional
Select Committee on Shipping Board
operations, Of which Representative
Joseph Walsh of Massachusetts is
chairman, testified yesterday to the
losses which the Government has suf-
fered through exorbitant prices charged
for labor and material in repair work
and in the salvaging OF shipbuilding
plants.


Charles +. Hanes, an assistant ex-
aminer in the port Of New York for
the Emergency Fleet Corporation. told
of one case where he went aboard a
tug that was undergoing repairs. The
men were working in the small wire
less room, which could not possibly
have held more than three men, and
yet there were twelve men on board
and full time was allowed for all
twelve.


He recalled the case of the ship
Woyaca, where twenty-three men
went on board one Monday morning
and remained there until the follow
ing Monday. The company charged
the Government thirty-nine hours a
day per man for the whole week, and
the bill was allowed.

spread.

now most closely watched for and

pneumonia. The papers recently an

try was threatened with bolshevism.

LONDON. April 27.-French troops
reoccupied the village of Aintab. Asia
Minor. Monday, according to a Con-
stantiAople dispatch received bv Reut-
ers Limited.


Forces supporting Mustapha Kemal,
the Turkish Nationalist leader. have
cut the Bagdad Railway north and
south of the Cilician gates. where some
lighting has occurred, and in which
several Italian workmen have been
killed and others made prisoner.
French detachments have repaired the
railway between Mersinas and Adana,
which was cut by Turkish forces.


PARIS, April 27.-The latest infor-
nation received at the Foreign Office
from Asia Minor indicates that the
losses to the French troops at Urfa,
northwest of Mesopotamia, were less
serious than at first supposed. A large
detachment is thought to have got back
into the town. while others escaped in
various directions. The official version
attributes the French reverse to
treachery.


The force occupying Urfa comprised
700 men, of whom two companies were
white French troops and the rest Sene-
galese rifiemen. Reports to the War
Office indicate that the total loss was
200 killed.

third time Mrs. Elizabeth Blake, noted
spiritualist medium, has been pro-
nounced dead in her home in Coryville,
a suburb. After apparently dying twice
in the last three weeks, only to return
to life and repkove her dead husband,
Zachariah Blake, for allowing her to
leave him in the spirit land, Mrs. Blake
again was pronounced dead last night,
according to announcement Of her ply
sician.


Many of the mediums close friends
declared they did not believe the re-
port. "She will come bac:.,: :hey said.
But after lapse of twenty-four hours
there is no sign of returning conscious
ness.


Mrs. Blake, seventy-t two years old,
was stricken with pneumonia three
weeks ago. A week later she appar-
emily died, and for eight hours was
in state of coma She afterward told
friends she had been with her husband
and eleven children, all dead, and talked
of the beautiful spirit world"


Last Wednesday she again was pro-
nounced dead. There was no sign of
pulse beat. Preparations for the
funeral were begun, and newspapers
were provided with an obituary. But
again the aged medium startled per-
sons in the death chamber by opening
her eyes and beginning to talk Since
then she had been in a weak state, and
her death was regarded as imminent,

A LII day long where the sunlight gladdens
n Rock and headand, and beach and shoal,
White as the fierce salt surf that whitens
Crested breakers that shoreward roll,
Hither, thither, with brave breasts buoyant,
Loiter the gulls from near and far,
Now aloft on their spreading pinions,


Now wings folded on beach and bar.
Salt airs breathing and lungs expanded,


Thus I watch them till day grows dim;
Nigh and distant, the great sea, psalming,
Lifts triumphant a ceaseless hymn.
Back from the shore when the shadows


lengthen,


Far, far homing, before the night.
Sunset tinting their wings with color,


West west ever, they take their fight.
Far, far westward the gulls go speeding,


League and league through the dying day,
Till. low specks on the western skyline,


Faint and fainter, they fade away.
Birds, brave birds, when your fight is ended
Darkness yelling the rose red vest,
Stars above you. and night surrounding,


Where, oh, where do you take your restf
Where ! know not but this I witness


Dawnlight flooding the landscape fair),
Eastward flying, your snow white legions


Course their way through the dewy air.
Back again to the white sea -surges,


Back again ere the world awake
Brave breasts buoyant and wings extended
East. east ever your course ye take.
-Rodcric Quinn, in the Sydney Bulletin.

magistrate of Dublin Castle, was

Andrew Bonar Law. government
spokesman. announced his murder

street and shot him.

filled with passengers. AS it ap-
preached the Masonic school four
pen Ieaped into the street. forced

ish forces.

MacCurtain, Lord Mayor of Cork,
and prominent Sim Fein leader,
aroused the country. Sim Fem
leaders blamed the British police
for his murder.

most daily throughout Ireland. Po-
lice barracks have been attacked
and many constables murdered.
Government forces blamed the Sim
Fein for these outrages.


Dispatches yesterday reported
government agents had discovered
a quantity of firearms being smug-
gled into Ireland from Germany,
presumably to start a Sim Fein
rebellion.

WASHfNGTON. July l.-Poss bly,
the most signal examples of military
heroism since the armistice were Off
clally recognized here to-day wnen
Major General John A. Lcieune, the

Extraordinary heroism, conspicuous

alte had terrorized the small republic

Information reached the regional

provincial town Of Grande Rivere.

selves by backing their faces and

quarters near Capois.


Disguise Proves Effective


The Americans, with their men trail

Haytian hills through terrain they knew

finally reached the first outpost guard

lowed them to pass after a cursory eX-
animation. Four more outposts were
passed IN the same manner-w without
incident. The sixth outpost was Peralte s
immediate guard and the bandit, him
self, was seen within thirty PAGES OF
the sentries.


Believing the arrivals were runners
returning with news of the attack on
Grand Riviere, Peralte allowed Hen
neken and Button to advance to within
a few feet Of his person before he and
his sentrleS senSed something wrong
Hanneken was armed with two govern
ment automatics and Button had q
light Browning machine gun. Without
further ceremony, the two Americ leans
opened fire. Henneken killed the ban
dit chief instantly and Button devoted
his attention TO the bodyguard. But
tons score was nine.

night During the day of November
they fought their way back to marine
head quarters, encountering and dis

on Grand Riviere.

months ago the Navy Department saw

dropped into the ocean. With Mrs,
Dalton and her, daughters in the

Ridge.

along the shore road when a small
girl ran in front of the machine.

the car went over the bank. Mrs.
Dalton, her daughters, Miss Lee and

the auto. which overturned, but
were quickly rescued by life guards.

at the point where the cars plunged
over the bank. All OF the party
were taken to the Coney Island
Hospital and after treatment they
went home with the exception of
Miss Lee. She was submerged
somewhat longer than the others.

LAREDO, Tex, May o.-Nuevo La
redo, the Mexican town opposite this
city. surrendered to rebel forces at 7
o'clock this morning after a two hours
battle. Three Federal defenders and
one rebel soldier were killed. The re-
volutionists attacked from three sides
Of the town.


General Reynaldo CARA commander
of federal forces in the Nuevo Laredo
military district. tonight is refugee
on American soil. Following defeat Of
mis- troops and capture of Nuevo Laredo
by revolutionists early to-day the Car
ranza officer arrived in Laredo to-
night and took refuge in the Mexican
Consulate.


General Cara, who ordered his
troops to make a determined stand
against the rebel attack on Nuevo
Laredo at dawn. saw his defense
erumpled after short fight and with
his son escaped in an automobile. Pur-
sued by rebels, the general eventually
forded the Rio Grande, five miles west
of Nuevo Laredo and arrived on
American soil with his automobile per
forated by bullets.


Nuevo Laredo Celebrates Surrender


The revolutionists approached Nuevo
Laredo shortly before dawn from the
west and drew the Federal force on
that side. About one hundred mounted
rebels then entered the town from the
south and east When they reached
the center of the city the Federal gar
1ison began to fire into the air and
surrendered without serious resistance
The casualties occurred in the western
outskirts during the first stages of the
attack.


The most resistance, however, took
place in the section Immediately sur
rounding General Garzas residence
This probably was for the purpose OF
covering the Federal commanders es-
cape, it was said. The number of men
involved in the battle could not be
ascertained.


When the rebels had taken full con
troll of the town the populace turned
cut in celebration Bands paraded the
streets playing popular marches, while
the crowds cheered.

prices ever known in this market. The
highwater mark was reached Tues
day when three lots from the West
ern shore OF Virginia brought $2.75
a dozen straight through for primes,
mediums and culls. on the wharf here.
This price was exclusive of the pack
age, which brought the price up to
sass. when packed ready for ship
ment.


The extreme scarcity has prevailed
since the season first opened, early
in May, and from present Indications
will continue until late in July or
early in August. There have been but
very few crabs caught in the
waters near Crisfeld. and crabs that
have been shipped from here, totaling
perhaps less than one-fourth of the
normal shipments, are practically all
from the Western Shore.

TOXIC. October 12.-The economic
crisis in Japan has had the result Of i'm
mensely quickening the time for trans
mission of cablegrams between Japan
and the United States. A falling Nofr
in business means less crowded cable
and message that took ten days and
over during the war now go through in
less than twenty-four hours.


Tho ministry of communications has
Cancelled the war decree giving the
same person the right to send only one
urgent cablegram per day. Any one
may now send an unlimited number of
urgent messages. Such cablegrams are
always restricted to ten words and cost
three times the ordinary commercial
messages.

BOLOGNA, Italy, Dec. GA serious
clash occurred yesterday at Ferrars,
t" "enty-seven miles rorth of Bologna.
where the Socialists had organized e.
demonstration in protest against the
recent attacks in Bologna upon Social
ist Deputies. Four persons were killed
and more than thirty were wounded be :
tore the police and troops, who were
rushed to the spot, restored order. Fiji
teen Red Guards, who were among.a
large number who had fired upon the
Nationalists from the confines of the
adjacent medieval castle, were arrest
ed. The other Red Guards escaped.


1t was thought that thorough pre-
cautions had been taken by the police
and the military to obviate trouble.
These preparations were thought to
have been necessary because Of the ar
rival OF commission Of the Chamber
Of Deputies which was empowered to
investigate the recent disorders.


Socialists Pledged Order


More than 10000 persons gathered
for the Socialist demonstration. The
Socialist leaders, it was said, had
pledged their word that no untoward
incidents would occur. The authorities
believed the absence Of police and
carabineers from the scene would con-
tribute to avoid incidents.


The Socialists held their mass meet
ing in the Communal Theater, which
was decorated with red flags. In the
royal box the court Of arms of the
House Of Savoy was replaced by q por-
trait of NikOlai Lenine, the Russian
Soviet Premier.


While the meeting was in full swing
600 Nationalists in military formation
issued from their quarters near the
theater, intending to carry out pa
rade through the streets and to sing
war songs and shout the war cry Of
Gabrielle d'Annunzio At first the Ma
tionalists were confronted by male
nurses from the lunatic asylum. These
nurses, all Socialists, marched in the
opposite direction to the Nationalists,
waving red flags.


Red Guards Open Fire


Then Il volley of rife fire swept over
the Nationalists, the shots coming
from the battlements Of famous
neighborlng medieval castle. The
castle, which was the seat Of the So
cialist Provincial Council. had been
occupied from carly morning by Red
guards, who had come there from vari-
GUS parts of the province to be ready
for any contingency.


When the firing began there was
great excitement and stampede OF
the people imm mediatcly followed. Dur
ing the shooting, which continued ONLY
for a few minutes, the screams of the
horror-strcken people could be heard
above the volleys from the rifles When
order finally was restored the troops
rushed into the castle and took into
custody fifteen persons, but the others
who had been inside had escaped

For the last two weeks there have
been cast up along the Jersey and
Long Island shores thousands of phials,
filled with white powder and her
metically sealed-phials which little
children have found explode like minia-
ture bombs when hurled against rock


The phials contain calcium hydro
chlorite, a preparation used during the
war to purify water


But tonight only half the mystery
was solved Having identified the
phials as part of those made in the
United States and incased in vacuum
tubes for shipment overseas for use
by individual soldiers, the authorities
are still unable to answer the question
OF how, more than two years after
fighting had ended, the phials came to
be washed ashore at summer resorts.


The most logical conclusion, that
cases containing tie water purifier had
been hurled overheard or that a ship
bearing them overseas had been sunk
or this coast, met no support from
army transportation officers here. The
only theory substituted was that mys-
terious ocean currents had brought
back to these shores, after two years,
phials lost in the torpedoing of some
transport on the other side of the At
lantic.

BERLIN, Aug. l9.-The eight hour
street battle last night between French
soldiers and German civilians in Kat
towitz, in the so-called plebiscite area
Of Upper Siiesia, may give rise to in
ternational complications.


The fighting began early yesterday
evening and continued until O'Clock
this morning. The French used tanks
and armored cars. The exact casu.
alties are not known, but according
to the latest figures ten French
soldiers and twenty-five Germans were
killed and about seventy wounded on
both sides. Public feeling in the town
and adjoining territory is running high
and the population Is reported to have
called upon the French troops to hand
over their arms.


Berlin Press Alarmed


The Berlin press expresses alarm lest
France may hold the German govern
ment responsible. Martial law has
been proclaimed in Kattowitz and the
surrounding district. Postponement of
the plebiscite, whereby the population
is to determine whether it will ioin
Germany or Poland, coupled with COM
plants against the conduct of the
French troops, had already led to
strained relations III the district, and
the public bitterness was increased by
charges that the French had been
smuggling arms and munitions into
Poland from the plebiscite area.


AS protest against such an allege d
breach of neutrality a strike was pro
claimed yesterday at Kattowitz, and
early in the evening the strikers went
to demonstrate before the Offices of
the inter-Allied commission. 1t is al
legged that the French fired on the dem
onstrators. Fierce fighting soon became
general IN the town and many buildings
were burned.

Gordon, cieverly disguised.

tionalist agitator, not excluding Mus
tapha Kemal himself. For years she

the allies and preaching Turkish ma
tionalism. She was the first Turkish
woman to be trained at the American
Roberts College and was the first war
nurse in the Ottoman empire.

NEW YORK, Dec. 26.-Police to-
night were vainly seeking a motive
for the murder and suicide of two
Young women. owners of the Little
Beauty ParIor" at 361 Van Brunf
street, Brooklyn. both of whom were
found dead in the shop this after
noon.


They were Miss Anna Donegan, a
decorated war nurse, 80 years old,
and Mrs Edna Hague, a widow, 20
years old. The body of the former
Law across that of Mrs. Hague. while
Miss Donegan still held clasped in
her right hand a United States army
Colt automatic revolver.


From the position of the bodies,
the police believe Miss Donegan shot
and killed Mrs. Hague and then took
her own life. Mrs. Hague was shot
twice. One bullet entered her brain
lust back of the right ear and the
second penetrated the center of her
forehead. Miss Donegan had been
shot through the mouth. the bullet
taking an upward course and pierre
ing her brain.


Both women were we'll know4 in
the neighborhood and their shop Vas
patronized by many well known
Brooklynites. Their business was
prosperous and they had no apparent
reason for a quarrel, according to
neighbors.


The young women were good look
ing and each about 80 years old. No
notes were found.


A notice on the door announced
it would be closed today and the
presence of the women in the shop
attired in their street clothes is an
other angle to the mystery. No one
had seen them enter.


The shots were heard shortly af-
ter noon and the police notified.
They found the bodies of the women
after smashing down the door.


Police tonight located Miss Done
gan's sister, Kathryn, who told of
the partnership and declared her
sister was worried over Mrs.
Hague's plan to leave and marry.

close somewhere, this history of Jen-

The meat diet of the average Amer
ican family is made up principally of
beef. pork and mutton. OF these
three. beef and pork are by far the
more popular. Mutton. which for a
long time was not extensively used,

popularity.


The reason is evident The human
scores Of enticing beef and pork

together different kind of meat. and

ways


The ordinary cuts of mutton and
lamb are perhaps not as familiar as
those of beef and pork. Sheep and
lambs are divided into fore-quarters
and hind d-quarters. The hind quarters
are known to the trade as saddles and
the fore quarters as market cut racks
The saddles are divided into legs and
mutton loin. while the hotel cut loin
has the flank trimmed off and the
kidney removed.


. The fore-QuarterS are made up of
hotel rack and stew. stew being some
times divided into chucks and wings
know them, come from the loins and
the hotel cut rack. The hind legs
furnish the famous roasts of leg Of
mutton or lamb. The well known
lamb and mutton stews come from the
chucks and wings.


There is great variety of other
products of lamb and mutton which
the average household sees only in
frequently and yet they make marvel
Gus dishes that will delight the most
epicurean tastes. For instance. there
are sheep tongues. heads and brains.
lamb sweetbreads and fries. sheep
kidneys and piucks. These parts are
only a small portion of the entire
animal, but they are not rare or ex-
pensive. because they are not in uni
versal demand.

few hours later took charge Of the

neck with hangpan's knot the body

Island.


Tho girl was well dressed and the

believe that she was of French ex-
traction. An absence of bruises or
rents in the clothing led them to believe
that she might nave hanged herself

breaking of the cord had caused her
to fall into the position in which she
was found, but the darkness of the
woods at the time the discovery
was made was such that it was impos-
sible to make a thorough investigation
of tho place.


This darkness and the thickness of
the leaves about the spot where the
girl lay also prevented the police from
examining the ground very carefully, so
that they could not state definitely last
night whether or not there were any
Indications OF a struggle having taken
place.


The presence of the body was at first
reported 10y two young men of West
New Brighton. who had come upon 1t
sfter dusk. They were Edward Schnei-
der of ESQ Pelton avenue and Raymond
Schreisner OF Is Seneca avenue. They
reported the matter 10 the police OF the
West New Brighton police station.


When force of policemen and de-
tectives under Acting Captain Ernest
Van Wagner went to the place with the
Young men darkness had set In and at
first they could not find tho spot. but
after procuring lanterns and wandering
about for more than two hours the
officers discovered the body.


The girl's hair was light brown, her
eyes blue, and she had weighed about
1875 pounds. Her height was five feet
five inches. She was attired in blue
serge dress of good quality, trimmed
with black and brown beads. yellow
satin underskirt over a white muslin
underskrt, pink flannelette boomers.
black silk openwork stockings. and
brown oxfords. white corduroy tur-
ban trimmed with black and white
beads lay near the body.


From the fact that the body was not
covered with leaves the police immedi-
ately inferred that the girl could not
have laid there long. This was also the
belief of DR.. George Mord. county
medical examiner. who later looked at
the body and said that in all probability
the girl had not been there for more
than about sixty hours. He thought
that she had been dead for forty-eight
hours at least. The spot where the body
was found is about 500 feet from the
nearest street or roadway and is on
one of the highest points on Staten
Island

With nine thousand miles of hard
ships and dangers behind them four
weather battered planes In squadron
formation came roaring over New York
city yesterday about one O'Clock. AS
the planes flew toward Mineola they
were met by flotilla Of thirty other
planes and escorted in triumph to safe
landing at Mitchell Field.


The eight brown young men In the
battered airplanes had accomplished the
aeronautical impossible. They had flown
safely over thousands OF miles OF the
widest part of the American continent.
through snow. rain and fog. TO Nome.
their machines, sorely tried by rougn
landings and mishaps on many rough
fields. and flown back again.


The only people among the hundreds
who welcomed the hiers at Mitchell Field
who were not profoundly impressed by
the exploit were the fliers themselves.
They JSyfully unloaded one small billy
goat and six small but exceedingly
lively Alaskan dogs besides piles of
trophies and gifts with which enthusi-
astic Alaskans had burdened their
planes and told funny stories about
things that had happened along the way.
one biz Of news they brought was that
every Alaskan has his own private Still.


The men who made the long trip and
regarded their hardships and dangers SO
lightly were Capt. ST. Clair Street. COM
mander of the squadron; Lieut. Ross c.
Kirkpatrick, Lieut.. c. III. Crumrine
: 10, Nuft iHuf Eric Nell
son, Capt. Howard Douglas, Sergeant
Joseph L. English and Sergeant James
Long.


Fought Every Kind of Weather


The flight TO the Behring Sea and
back was a struggle against unusually
bad weather, as we'll as against rough
country. doubly dangerous because II
was unknown economically and very
sparsely settled The first day Of the
flight July Is. the fiiers ran into rain
before they had reached Jersey, and
when the planes took off yesterday from
Erie. Pa. they did so in the midst of fog
and murk.


Time and time again fog separated
the squad into individual units. with the
pilots desperately fighting the white
mist which robbed them Of their sense
OF equilibrium and cloaked mountain
peaks and forests from sight. once
Capt Streets plane caught fire in the
air, but he side slipped and managed to
extinguish the fire. The planes were
sometimes lost, sometimes suffered
broken axles. blown tires, smashed run
ming gear broken propellers and leaky
gas tanks. but somehow the men got
their machines through the worst mis-
haps successfully.


In actual flying time the 5000 mile
trip consumed fifty-six hours each way
On sixteen days the fiers actually made
progress In flight to Alaska, ana or
fifteen days were able to take to the air
to head for MIneola. All the rest OF
the time, practically since July 10. has
been spent in waiting on weather. Capt
Street In recounting the story of the
flight said that the planes maintained ar
average height OF 5000 feet but in pass
ing over the Canadian Rockies were
compelled at times TO rise AS high as
49, 900 feet. Two thousand miles OF
territory were flown over where a forced
landing, possibly with injuries 10 the
crew. meant a foot Journey OF 200 miles
or more to the neares. habitatlon.


Telegraph Creek. i. c.. was unani-
mously accorded the worst reputation
Of all for weather and general cussed-
ness. Here. onGthe return trip, three
Of the niers waited nineteen days for re-
pairs 70 Lieut.. Cumrime's plane and for
possible flying weather. Three unsuc-
cessful attempts were made to leave.
Each time impossible weather drove
them back to the Telegraph Creek Field.


Indians Not Impressed.


Capt. Street said that the widest en-
thusiasm was manifested everywhere in
Alaska and citizens planned 10 make
strong demands for air mail service,
especially in sections where any other
mode OF travel Is impossible at some
seasons OF the year. The Indians were
the only sceptics concerning the new
means of travel. One frank chief told
Capt. Street he was damn smart but
damn fool


Much valuable data was gathered dur
ing the trip which will be turned over
to the Geological Survey when the fliers
go TO Washington tomorrow. Maps
made from material furnished by trap
pers. were found to be decidedly inaccu-
rate. and drawings and photographs will
be submitted for the purpose of correct
ing these. Some mountains marked as
being only 5000 feet high forced the
filters up to IL. 900 20 clear them.


Capt. Street said that the path blazed
by the Alaskan squadron could be made
practical for airplanes by a few improve
ments IN landing fields, and that a large

much better time with normal weather
conditions Mail which takes thirty days

where q linen shirt. silk stockings
