PARIS, March 25.-No matter how
many treaties are signed or not
signed, world peace will not be estab-
Iished until Central Europe and the
Near East are thoroughly clcansed
and disinfected. Henry i. Dawson,
head Of the American Red Cross, de-
clared today.


"Ninety-nine per cent OF the peo-
pies of the world do not care
damn about the signature or ratifica-
ton of treaties, but care Immensely
for their safety from the seourges
now sweeping eastern Europe and
Asia. and which constitute the
mightiest danger to all humanity
since the deluEe.


America is just as unsafe as Eu-
rope from typhus and the white
plague now spreading over tho world
with lightning rapidity.


Two million three hundred thou
sand infected Russian refugees are
now pressing against western Eu-
ropes borders in their mad rush
westward. in the hope of escaping
death under the most horrible con
ditions.


"A ship carrying two full-fedged
generals, seven brigadier generals.
twenty-four colonies and 200 troops
from Russia Is even now rowing the
Mediterranean, rejected at every port
like hopeless pilgrim, unable to
land her infected cargo. The ulti-
mate fate of this modern phantom
ship cannot be foretold.


"Whole populations are being wiped
out. The fatal germs pass from one
country to another, owing to- the
lack of sanitary devices. Unless
quick relief is provided the world
will see a tragedy greater than that
of the last five years"

An attractive run of 200 miles,
through the most charming sections of

returning along Great Peconc Bay

Jefferson, Oyster Bay and Roslyn; a

lowing the trolley tracks into Hemp
stead. After crossing the railroad fol

right. Leave the track and after cross

short way. Then make a right turn

woeful, sobbing noise, when ups
give way to downs.

CHICAGO, March 29.--The death list
of the Palm Sunday tornadoes that
swept parts of eight states tonight
stood at 100.


Telegraph and telephone service with
many isolated communities in the
Middle West had only been partly re-
stored tonight, and indications were
that the toll of death and destruction
would be augmented.


The known dead in six Central West
ern states numbered los, while
ffty-fve were killed in Georgia
and Alabama. The property loss in
the Chicago area alone was estimated
at 100000 while in the other states
affected the material loss was large.
Elgin, H., suffered the heaviest prop
erty loss, the damage there being $4.-
100000.


Illinois was the hardest hit of the
Central states, with thirty dead, more
than 1000 injured and 1900 made
homeless.


Indiana Reports Thirty-six Deaths


Indiana reported thirty-siX fatalities
and Ohio twenty-siX. Eleven were
killed in Michigan and one each in Wis
consin and Missouri.


The districts most severely affected
in the Chicago area were Irving Park,
within the city limits, with six dead;
Melrose Park, nine dead; Elgin, eight
dead; haywood, four dead, and Plain
field, three dead.


Heavy property damage resulted IN
these towns, and also in Wilmette and
Evanston, North Shore suburbs. No IA
talities occurred in the latter places.


At Joliet, H., three persons probably
were fatally injured, fourteen were Sc
riously hurt and the property damage
was estimated at 100000.


Troops Patrol Streets


Troops patrolled the streets of Elgin,
Melrose Park and Wilmette to-day.


Health Commissioner Robertson Of
Chicago modified every available sur
geon and nurse and sent them to the
stricken areas Mayor Thompson acted
with the City Council in raising funds
by public subscription, and Red Cross
headquarters were opened. In several
places American Legion posts sent vol
unteers to watch for hooters and as
sist in relief work.


Henry J. Cox, weather forecaster for
Chicago, said the tornado was the re-
suit of combination of two storms
One developed in Alaska, travelled
through British Columbia and Joined g
storm from the southwest, which de-
veloped in the arid plateaus Of south
ern Arizona aud Nevada. This comb.
nation, Professor Cox said, resulted in
rotary motion which formed eddie.
and caused tornado.


Although the tornado travelled for
ward at rate of about fifty miles al
hour, the wind at the core of the tor
nado was estimated to have had
velocity of from 200 to 300 miles al
hour,

piication of the square deal to all citi-
zens and government subsidy for a

efficient business administration of the
country's affairs, speedy change in the
nations taxation system whereby the
burden would be more equally dis
tributed, better relation between labor
and capital, certain law and order
everywhere and measuring of the needs
of the nation by looking ahead, "but
with feet always on the ground"


Especially alone, President Wilson

nationality, and still essentially alone,
one in a hundred million, he blocks its

ng said the people of the South are

Sam Sherman's parrot, for the eighth
time, frustrated an attempt to ROB
Sans tailor shop and living quarters,
at 391 Pearl Street, last night.


The Sherman family's dining room is
on the ground floor behind the shop,
while the other living rooms are on
the floor above, whore the parrots cage
hangs


Last evening Sam, Mrs. Sherman and
their daughter Celia, twenty years
old, were just sitting down to supper
when they heard series of piercing
shrieks from Polly. They rushed out,
Celia in the lead, and discovered :.
young man fleeing from the hallway.
Celia gave chase and overlook him af-
ter two blocks, hanging on until De-
tectives Rowan and Riley, of the Oak
Street station, came to her assistance


The prisoner was taken to Police
Headquarters. He described himself
as Frank Fabelo, twenty-five years old,
with no fixed abode. The detectives
say a jimmy was found on him and
that it fitted into newly made dents in
Sherman's door jamb.


Seven burglars who preceded last
nights intruder in trying to break into
the Sherman home have been scared
away by Polly's outcries, the tailor
told the police.

All five Of the socialist members of
the New York state assembly. ousted
from that body last winter. were yes
terday reelected at special elections.
despite fusion that had been effected
in all the districts between the repub-
licans and the democrats. This re-
suit was due to the fact that on both
sides an extremely light vote was
polled, but the loss Of the fusion vote
over the combined republican and
democratic votes of last November
was much heavier than that Of the
socialist vote. In the five districts
last year 32,516 anti-socialist votes
were cast and 2S.469 socialist votes.
the socialist candidates winning
through the divisions Of the opposi-
tion to them. Yesterday in the same
districts 1885 anti-socialists were
cast for the fusion candidates and IT,
654 socialist votes were cast. Thus
the falling off in the fusion vote from
that cast last November was 21.1S0. as
against loss OF only 6.31S socialist
votes. This tells the story plainly.
Those opposed to the socialists were
not as much concerned over the cleo
ton as were the socialists. And yet
even the latter did not turn out In
their full strength. despite their vgor-
Gus campaigning and their appeals for
sympathy on the ground OF injustice.
It may be that the great explosion
downtown distracted attention from
the election sufficiently to make even
the depleted socialist vote heavier than
the evidently Indifferent anti-socialist
forces.

PHILADELPHIA, March 27.-Four
employees, of the Atlantic Refining
Company are dead and ten others are
reported injured as the result Of colli-
sion this morning between passenger
motor bus and Philadelphia & Read
ing Hog Island train.


Twenty men and three women en-
plcyees Of the oil company rode in the
bus. The accident occurred at Sixty
third Street and Gibson Avenue. Sixty
third street, approaching the railroad
at Gibson Avenue, is down grade. The
chauffeur and occupants of the bus saw
the train approaching when within 1O1
feet from the railroad. The passengers
shouted to the chauffeur to apply the
brakes. The wheels refused to grip
the slippery grade. The chauffeur
twisted the steering gear sharply. The
heavy bus careened on two wheels,
righted and crashed sidewise into a
warning signal pole.


The collision failed to halt the bus,
which sideswired the second coach Of
the train and overturned. None of the
bus passengers had an opportunity to
jump. Several of them were thrown
clear of the wreckage. Others were
caught under it.

first Of the many Darby youths to vol
unteer, Demster was in France ready
for action within short time after war
was declared.


On July 10, 1918, when the Allies
took the offensive, after the Americans
had held the line against the Germans,
Demster was wounded In the leg while
delivering a message under heavy fire.
After recovering from his wounds he
was wounded by an exploding shell,
being sent home he has undergone sew
eral operations in the hope of saving
his remaining eye, the last of which was
performed few days ago.

BELLPORT, L. L., Friday.--One robber
was wounded in fusillade of shots ex-
changed between five men and scores OF
residents early this morning when the
safe of the Post Office here was blown
open for the fourth time in eight years
and looted OF about 5000 in cash and
stamps. The robbers escaped in a high
powered automobile.


Tools, a soft green hat and fingerprnts
left by the safe robbers furnish additional
clues. The police investigation shows that
the men arranged the details of the rob-
berry with great care. An automobile,
with a chauffeur and with the engine run
ming, was standing in front of the Post
Office while lookout was posted out
side the building. He gave the alarm
when Constables Thomas Valentine ana
his son. Thomas, Jr., approached the
Post Office.


The high explosive charge used by the
robbers blew the safe door across the Of
flee and imbedded il into the wall. The
front of the building was demolished. and
windows in the vicinity were shattered.


Miss Helen Rabbit, niece of Mrs. Charles
e. Osborne, whose home is opposite the
Post Office, saw the robbers drive UP to
the Post Office and enter the building She
notified the police.


Before they arrived, however. the blast
went off. The man on watch saw the
Valentines and called to his three COM
panions inside the building. when all the
robbers ran for their automobile.


Constable Valentine and his son opened
fire when they saw the men escaping. O1e
of the safe blowers cried I'm hit" and
dropped his tools. which consisted OF
sledge hammer two crow bars and
searchlight. The others helped him into

GREENVILLE, Me-. March IA
Robert C. Moore died tonight and his
wife is wounded seriously as the result
Of an attack upon them at their home
last night According to Mrs. Moore,
two men entered the house, forced their
way upstairs to room where her hus-
band was taking bath and opened
fire upon him with revolvers.


Five Of the bullets took effect, one
entering Moore's abdomen, two pene-
trating his chest and two striking his
arms. Mrs. Moore said that as her
husband fell unconscious the men fired
at her. She was wounded in the hand
and one bullet entered each of her
arms. She was able to get to the out
side door and shout for help. Mean
while the men ran off.


Mrs. Moore said the two men were
William Pomeroy and j. C. Scott, who
came here from New York last Tuesday
to work as woodsmen. Deputy Sheriff
Rogers learned that Pomeroy and Scott
had boarded freight train bound for
Canada, and on his orders they were
arrested tonight without resistance
before they reached the border.


Robbery was given as the probable
motive for the crime When the men
were arrested they had no weapons.
They refused to make any statement
They will be taken to the Jail at Dover
tomorrow

May day found the trees Of the cap
ital nearly in full leaf and with two
or three sunny days the trees of the
streets and parks will be clothed in
all the glory Of their green. The
naples, willows, aspens, poplars, lin
dens and the elms began making their
spring toilet a month ago, but the
autumnal chill and March capers of
April held their enthusiasm in check.
The more cautious or the less demon
strative trees-the red oaks and the
pin oaks-are thinking Of putting on
their vernal finery, and now that May
is here they, too, will soon be robed
in foliage.


Out in the country the trees are not
so far advanced in green as their city
cousins. Country trees know more
about the weather than city trees and
are inclined to take fewer chances.
They are slower-going and less specula-
tive than city trees and cannot be
wooed into leaf by few spring smiles.
They practice watchful waiting till the
sun comes farther north. But even
the country woods are fast changing
from brown and gray to green. The
great family of oaks that live in woods
near Washington-the white. post,
overcup, swamp white, COW, red, scar
let, black, black jack, single, willow
and Spanish-are permitting their lit
tie leaves to peep and take their first
glance at the spring skies. The black
walnut and the butternut, moekernut
and pignut hickories are turning greer.
and the large-tooth aspen, the river
birch, sweet birch, beech, blue beech
and the ashes, black, white and red, are
coming out Of their winter sleep. The
red maple, redbud, dog~ood, the shad-
husk and the nannyberry look like big
bouquets in the landscape. The old
familiar sassafras and witch hazel are
in golden flames, and the locust is
nearly ready to unfold its sweet white
blossoms. The persimmen, the black
gum and Eastwood are preparing to
furnish shade, and the red mulberry,
huckberry, sweet magnolia, yellow
poplar, black gum, red gum and paw
paw are coming into life to swell the
bright green army Of trees. And all
the orchards are dressed in pink and
white.

Brussels, June 1s.-The scream Of
factory sirens and the happy laugh
ter Of the people are driving the
echoes of the war from the heart Of
Belgium.


This is the Land That Has Come
Back"


People Are Happy.


Cross the Belgian frontier and you
are in a country of milk and honey
and among a people happy in indus
try and merry at play.


Belgium is recovering more rap
idly than any other European ma
ton from the effects of war. She
is fast regaining the place she held
in 1914.


This city is brilliant with electric
light Larger. better locomotives
draw Belgian trains than any others
on the continent. There are dining
cars and they serve good food.


Farmers Prosperous.


The fields through which you pass
are better kept and the farmers are
busy. Milk. eggs and butter are
plentiful.


The famous Belgian candymakers
have re-opened their shops and
Brussels streets are llneo Win can
dy and pastry shops.


The women's shops are hlled with
the loveliest fabrics and the smart
est and prettiest hats. They are
selling them, too.


Soup Kitchens Gone.


I visited a general store here, not
one that caters to the wealthy.


The prize delicacies of the world
were there-fresh fruits of every
cline. great blushing red sausages
of queer name and cheeses of
queerer shapes and much queerer
odors.


The American soup kitchen lives
in memory only.


The streets at nights are thronged
with crowds of well dressed laugh
ing people.


Behind these gay things are the
gray wheels of industry.


Railroads Rebuilt.


When the Germans left Belgium
they left chaos. The two things a
country must have to be prosperous
were missing-transport and
fuel


State engineers and army engi-
neers pitched in to rebuild and now
hardly a red line that means a
railway destroyed is left on the
maps.

HALIFAX, Feb. 1S.--Arctic ice packs,
literally black with walrus, seals and
other polar creatures, are the largest
within memory, according to reports
brought here by sailors and overland
travellers. The solid ice extends fur
ther south than at any time within
years, with the bays and inlets firing
ing the Newfoundland coast locked
tightly. The solid pack extends eight
miles south of Wainwright, 100 miles
north of Point Lay.


Newfoundland is icebound and rail-
roads are completely tied up. Inhab-
itants in the interior are suffering in
tensely and several deaths from expo
sure have resulted. Communication be-
tween settlements is impossible except
by dogsleds.


Reports of strange malady have
been received from Gander Bay, which
is without doctor. The disease is an
affection of the throat and has claimed
many lives, particularly children.

were rescued.

water by bridge workmen. She was
not seriously injured Other bridge
employees carried the children to
safety.

Junction. The railroad track offered
the shortest route. When they reached
the middle of the span the express
dashed into view. Miele stood dazed
as he heard the train approach He
was fifty-two years old.

In a fit of jealousy Emil Coudry,
custom house checker, shot his wife
Catharine, and daughter Mary, in
chase through their home at 274 Bed
ford Street yesterday.


The daughter, who is twenty-one. is
in critical condition at St. Vincent's
Hospital from bullet wounds in her
right jaw and abdomen The wife. who
is forty-two, lost her right ear. Coudry
told the police he twas tired the way
things had been going for the last two
years and couldn't stand their actions
any longer" After killing his family
he declared he had planned suicide.
Mrs. Coudry said that she and her
daughter always dressed alike and were
frequently taken for sisters. This she
thought caused her husband to become
jealous.


Coudry is forty-four The shooting
started about o'clock in the morning
when he entered the bedroom of his
wife and daughter and, mun.bling some
thing, opened fire on them with a ro-
volver. The first shot tore away Mrs.
Coudry's ear.


AS Mary jumped from bed and
screamed she was shot in the jaw.
Mother and daughter then fed through
the apartment. AS they entered the
dining room the girl turned and was
shot in the abdomen. She swooned,
but her mother picked her up and
dragged her out into the hallway and
into the apartment of Mrs. Jennie
Gusrnieri, where the girl regained con-
seriousness.


Coudry banged on the locked door
for time and finally broke it down.
The women fed and were running
downstairs when Coudry fired another
shot. On the way down Mrs. Coudry
says she saw her husband stop at the
second landing and reload his gun.
Just before they reached the door lead
ing to the street Coudry fired again.


Mrs. Coudry and her daughter ran
into neighboring house and were
given first aid treatment. In the mean
time a large crowd gathered, including
Policeman James Dunn and Detective
Ryan, of the Charles Street police sta
tion. They went to the Coudry apart
ment and in response to knocks were
admitted. When asked for the gun
Coudry pointed to bureau drawer, in
which the pistol was found. One shell
had been exploded.


Coudry was taken to the Jefferson
Market Court and was held by Mag
istrate Robert C. Ten Eyck without
bail for examination on Thursday.

today from that city by the Kokusai
Agency. The consul and his wife. ac
companied by British officer. were
walking through the outskirts of
Vladivostok when they were accosted
by six men. who took their valuables
and escaped.


On the same day Russian bandits.
riding in two automobiles. entered the
city. They fired upon the militia who
attempted without success to capture
them. In the confusion the militia
directed their fire upon the Japanese
post office. This brought Japanese
troops, who captured the militia.
They were released, however, when
the situation was explained.

Silent" the prisoner at the Charles
town state prison who has maintained
an unbroken silence for the last ten
years, was freed to-day, and he broke
that long silence with just one word,
Sure" Then he lapsed into silence
again, answering all questions and
making all his queries with q paper
and pencil. For twelve hours after his
release he had not uttered another
word.


Neither his meeting with relatives
as free man nor the sight of the
strange things that have come TO pass
IN the outside world since the prison
doors closed upon him twenty-five
years ago unloosened the tongue Of
Patrick ]. Hanley. After an artomo-
bile ride around the city, Hanley went
to the home of his sister. in Clifton
dale, tonight. He had said nothing
up to the time he went to bed.

side of the foot.

BERLIN, July BIN Graz, Austria,

high price of cherries. Cherry time

ditions similar to those in Graz. In
several German cities the people have
rioted over the high prices. exas-
perated beyond the limit of endurance
by seeing trees loaded with fruit.
Scarcely day passes without news
of food riots and violent deaths in
Hamburg. Cuxhaven. Wurzburg and
other cities in all parts of Germany.
The situation is bad because the pres
ent is a period between the crops.
Different sections lack different sta
pies.


Berlin lacks potatoes. which form
the main food of the people. All of
the old crop has been consumed and
the new potatoes cannot be dug until
they have attained their full growth.
Bread is very scarce. The people are
not starved. but they are pinched-
Hoover's warehouse packages, once
thought high priced. are now being
devoured ravenously. For Germany
$500, 900 worth of these packages have
been distributed. The rising price of
the mark and the scarcity of food
have made the packages cheap.
One of the main reasons for Ger
manys food troubles is the stagna-
ton of business. The betterment of
the mark has made expectation i'm
possible. Workmen have been laid
off and money is scarce. Either wages
must drop or the mark fall before the
Germans can sell. When the mark
was low spectators bought foodstuffs
which is now impossible to sell at
the old value of the mark. Prices
have dropped slightly, but not enough
to make living appreciably cheaper.
The riots are not political.

lengthy string of red box cars and
dingy white refrigeration coaches clat-

court yesterday. She said she had

caught until she made the blunder OF
fainting twice within sight Of the
same policeman.

sixty-two, explained that going about
the streets in gaudy attire and with
a striking sign attached to the back
of her waist had proven good ad-
yertising stunt for various persons

introduced a highly realistic swoon
she doubled her value as a purveyor
of publicity.


Last night she chose TO work
among the downtown Saturday
throngs. When she threw an artistic
faint near Market street. tender
hearted Patrolman Frank Altman
helped to revive her. An hour later
she tainted at Smithfield and Diamond
streets, and Altman CHANGED to be
among those present. He eyed her
coldly and marched her to the Cen
trail station.


Magistrate Sweeney fined Mrs. Kay
So, and she announced her retirement
as fainter.

At 9:30 O'Clock last Saturday morn
ing Mrs. Emily May Favre, slender
dark-ha;red woman of thirty-four, while
, respondent over financial difficulties
shot and killed her twelve-year-old
daughter, Emily Margaret, IN their
room on the second floor of the Hotel
Ashton. 1912 Madison Avenue. The
muzzle of the revolver was pressed
against the little girls left breast and
the bullet entered her heart.
AT noon yesterday the room of Mrs.
Favre-No. 21-was entered and she
was found in bed. The body of her
daughter, clad in a silk night dress. Law
beside her. She confessed that she had
killed the child. and said she had
intended to end her own life, but had
lost her nerve.


During the time that elapsed from
the moment she shot her daughter until
the room was entered-more than fifty
hours-Mrs. Favre, with revolver be-
meath her pillow, lay beside the body
of her child. She was trying, she said,
to get courage to take her own life
She did not leave the room from Friday
night until l o'clock yesterday, nor did
she touch food.


Letter Tells of Her Purpose
In a letter which was mailed Friday
to Hector Jackson of the Hotel ST.
George, Brooklyn, Mrs. Favre declared
chat she was wretchedly unhappy, that
her funds we're exhausted and that she
intended killing Margaret, her only
Mr.. Jackson has been looking after her
interests in the estate Of her father,
New Orleans business man, who died
recently. The letter did not reach it's
destination until yesterday morning.
Carl Gerow, of Ills Gates Avenue, an
associate of Jackson, hurried to the
hotel With his arrival, Mrs Favre
appeared to find her courage and seized
the weapon under her pillow. Gerow
snatched the revolver from her grasp
and flung it to the floor.


The woman was arrested Suffering
from lack Of food. she tottered as she
stood in the center of the room. A
breakfast of pork chops, toast and tea
was sent to her, and Mrs. Favre, ap-
parently with perfect composure, ate
heartily. AS she drank her tea the
body of Margaret was taken from the
room.


When she had finished her meal Mrs
Favre, betraying not the slightest emo
ton, told the detectives that she was
ready to accompany them. She walked
to the East Eighty eighth Street sta
ton without assistance. She told the
police that she was a native of Eng
land, that her husband was Simon
Favre, of New Orleans, and that she
had been divorced for twelve years
She came to America when child.


Faces Charge of Homicide


She was questioned by Assistant Dis
trict Attorney p. Francis Mario and
held on charge of homicide. She will
be arraigned this morning in Harlem
court.


Mrs. Favre is Of slight build, has
dark eyes and an attractive personality.
Yesterday she was attired in dark
blue coat suit trimmed with fur, and
a black velour hat. She carried large
silver purse. 1t was said at the hotel
she had only SIG in her possession.


Mrs. Favre and her daughter came to
New York on October from New Or
leans and registered at the Hotel Ash
ton as miss Fanett and sister" 1t
was Mrs. Favre's ambition to play in
motion pictures. and she had chosen
this as her stage name. Since her ar
rival in New York she has supported
herself with the income from her
fathers business, but of late she has
been unable to obtain funds from this
source. A checking account in the
Empire Trust Company was exhausted


Mrs. Favre and her daughter were
assigned to an expensive room. Some
time later she gave up the room and
moved with her daughter to the second
floor.


Daughter Had Been iii


The little girl had lately been ser-
ously i'll and was indisposed when she
was shot. With her daughters eyes
closed, Mrs. Favre pressed the revolver
against the girls breast and pulled
the trigger.


Upon receipt of the letter ftom Mrs.
Gerow to telephone the woman nine-
diately. This Gcrow did. He talked
with her for several minutes, and in
this conversation she did not mention
the fact that she had slain Margaret.
Not satisfied with the information he
had received Gerow hurried to the
hotel. He explained the circumstances
to Leigh Walker, manager of the Hotel
Ashton.


Together Gerow and Walker went to
Room 21 and knocked on the door Mrs.
Favre assured them that everything
was "all right" and the men went
back downstairs. Gerow again called
Mrs. Favre's room. Convinced by her
hesitancy in replying to his questions
that something was wrong, he sum
moned Mr.. Walter and they paid a
second visit to the room. Gerow en-
tered and found the body of Margaret
on the bed.


"I've killed her." cried Mrs. Favre,
"and I'm going to kill myself"


Takes Weapon from Woman


Gerow took the revolver from her
and called the hotel manager, who had
remained outside.


All of Mrs. Favre's belongings had
been packed in small black trunk
at the foot of the bed. with the ex-
ception of a manicure set on the
dresser In her letter to Mr.. Jackson
she gave directions as to how the prop
erty should be distributed.


Mrs. Favre told Assistant District
Attorney Marie that she has not seen
her husband since the divorce action.
While being questioned at the police
station she was quiet and self-con-
tanned, speaking in calm decisive tones.

The real interest in Mike Gilhooley's

Patrolmen Henry Immen, Of the Web
ster Avenue police station, was shot
and killed shortly after / o'clock yes
terday morning at Bainbridge Avenue
and Gun Hill Road, the Bronx, by men
who had just robbed the store Of Philip
Moskowitz of tobacco, candy and sugar
worth not more than $40.


Five shots were fired at Inmen.
Three took effect. Apparently, after
he had been hit twice and had fallen,
his murderers stood over him and sent
another bullet into the top Of his skull.
They stood so close that the empty shell
from an army model Colt .45 automatic
was found in 1mmen's hair.


Shots Heard by Nurse


Miss Margaret B. Ferguson, a nurse
in the Montefore Home for Jewish IN
curables. diagonally across from where
the clatter Of five shots fred rapidly
early yesterday morning. She went to
window and says she saw two men
running south on cambridge Avenue.
She watched them turn into 210th
Street; then north to Steuben Avenue
and west to Jerome Avenue, where
houses cut off her view.


Meanwhile Barry Greenwald, night
clerk at the Montefore Home, had
heard the shots and had telephoned to
the police booth at Gun Hill Road and
Webster Avenue, where Patrolman John
Loughran, also Of the Webster Avenue
station, was on duty.


Loughran ran toward Bainbridge
Avenue and saw a sled standing in the
snow. Several bags were piled on it
and what appeared to be larger bag
lay beside it. As he drew near he
looked down into the face Of his friend
and station-mate, Immen.


The dead policeman's revolver was
still in its holster. His slayer had given
him no chance for his life. One bullet
had hit under Immen's left arm and had
passed down through his chest; another
had hit him on the left side of the ab-
domen. The third had driven down
through the top Of his skull.


Patrolman Died Instantly


An ambulance from Fordham Hospl-
tai was called, but the surgeon said
1mmen had died almost instantly. -Four
other empty shells were found near the
body, showing that the shots we're fired
at point blank range and confirming
the story of the Montefore Home en-
ployees that there had been five.


Investigation disclosed that the
'Markowitz shop had been rihed A
pane. Of glass had been broken from
the back door and the latch raised.
The sled on which the loot had been
piled was also stolen from the store.


Acting Captain Carey, of the Homi-
eide Squad; Acting Captain Duane, of
the Webster Avenue station; Assistant
District Attorney William Quigley and
a score Of detectives are working on
the case.


1ramer was thirty-eight years old
and rad been on the force since 1912.
ster Avenue. He has one son, Arthur.
two years old.

Two Essex touring cars, carrying U. S. Mail,
each one making the entire trip between San
Francisco and New York, have set the time
records for their respective directions across
the American continent


And thus comes to Essex another dstinc-
ton for reliability and endurance.


Except for one airplane record, these two
Essex cars have crossed the continent in less
time than was ever recorded by any travelling
machine. The fastest time possible between
San Francisco and New York by train is
slightly less than the time taken by the light
weight economical Essex. But in the case of
the railroad train, many different locomotives
are used, each pulling the train only a few
hundred miles.


From Cheyenne to Omaha the route taken
by the Essex was 43 miles longer than the
$50 mile route of the famous Overland Limited
yet the Essex time was but one hour longer
than the express train time.

marriage register.
